lg.l: [The confidante's] refusal [of the bard] at the door, [the bard] speaking at the door,
the confidante rebuking [the bard], [the bard's] vexation appearing,
the hero becoming vexed, the heroine becoming vexed,
[the heroine] saying “He, the lover, does not desire me”,
the mother seeing [this] and speaking, and other [situations] which exist

because of enduring love [are] 'the separation to that place'This, as is made clear in the commentary, is a way to refer to the hero's separation when he is visiting his extramarital lover, referred to in this translation as 'the other woman'. It is not clear however, exactly how to translate the phrase āyiṭai pirivu. The most common translations are 'intermediate-distance separation' or 'separation to that place'. The second is preferred in part due to its ambiguity. For the sake of clarity, āyiṭai is a combination of the deictic prefix 'a' (that, there) and the noun 'iṭai' (place). Both convey the idea that this separation is both short-term, at least compared to the long-distance version mentioned in the previous cūttiram, and short-distance, as the hero's other woman is understood to live in the same town as the hero and heroine by theoreticians. The translation 'that place' allows for an elliptical reference to the fact that he is going somewhere he shouldn't by stepping out of his marital home, and it also keeps open the possibility that it can be a separation to a place that is right there..

div.p: eṉpatu āy iṭaip pirivām āṟuṇarttutaṉutaliṟṟu.
The quoted [cūttiram] intends to make known the way in which 'the separation to 'that place' occurs.
vāyiṉ maṟuttal mutal ākac cevili kūṟṟīṟākac collap paṭṭa vivaiyum piṟavum parattaiyiṟ pirivām eṉṟa vāṟu.
Beginning with 'the refusal at the door' and ending with 'the foster-mother's speech', these which have been mentioned and others are 'the separation on account of the other woman'.
piṟavum eṉṟataṉāṟ parattaiyar kūṟṟum pūppuṇarttutalum uḷ ḷiṭṭaṉa vellāṅ koḷka.
By piṟavum, understand that they include all of the speeches of the other woman and 'the making known of menstruation'.

lg.l: Because you are a base man, the words from your mouth are lies.
Don't stand there bard. Leave now!

If our quarter sees [you] rushingpariyal could also be another negative imperative, — the same form that appears in TNV18-11 — in which case: “Don't grieve! If the town sees you...”. Another option is to take it as a verbal noun: “If the town sees you grieving, the man...”. Both those are less likely as the poem is clearly rebuking the bard. under the sun,
the man from town with vast paddy-fields will alsoIs the implication here that the hero will feel the same shame that the heroine would if the bard were spotted? obtain shame.

div.p: eṉpatu pāṇaṉukku vāyiṉ maṟuttatu.
[The confidante] refuses [entry] to the bard at the door.

lg.l: ... I do now speak of the goodness...

please don't beat me!This is only a partial translation, but it is possible as not much text is lost, and one can guess based on the length of missing chunk and its position, it was probably a phrase qualifying the 'goodness'.

div.p: eṉpatu vāyiṉ maṟukkappaṭṭa pāṇaṉ kūṟiyatu.
The bard, who had been refused at the door, speaks.

lg.l: The foolish woman with the brilliant forehead
does not remember what the man from the town did.
as though she had not experienced [it],
alas, she scolded me because of her angry disposition.

div.p: eṉpatu viṟali vāyiṉ maṟuttatu.
The dancing-girl refuses [the bard] at the door.
Too much has been lost to make a translation worthwhile.
eṉpatu tōḻikku vāyiṉ maṟuttatu.
[The bard] refutes the confidante at the door.

lg.l: As [her] red mouth quivered like the petals on the coral tree
as she thought, “Surely our protector will come here”,

the one with the beautiful long eyes became redThe normal connotation that reddining of the eyes has is sadness — eyes become red because of crying. cē-ttal, however, can also mean to become angry. Considering the other poems in this section, anger rather than sadness seems to be the dominant emotion experienced by the heroine. The poet may have been playing with this double connotation. that day.

div.p: eṉpatu vāyiṉ maṟuttamai tōḻi talaimakaṟkuc colliyatu.
The confidante speaks to the hero about the [the bard's] refusal at the door.

lg.l: O heart, we suffer so much!
I did not even get through the doorLit., “obtain the door”. Understood here are obtain entry at the door. a little bit at the feast.
The one with the perfect jewels will not give up [her] anger.

div.p: eṉpatu vāyil peṟāta talaimakaṉ vāṭiyatu.
The hero, who had not obtained [entry] at the door, grieves.

lg.l: Having gone [to her], I know of the one

who today thinksThe confidante can also be the agent of niṉaii, in which case she would feel bad about about what she said when refusing the hero (or the bard) entry to the house, and now wants make it up to him by helping resolve the lovers' quarrel. all the words spoken yesterday

a mistake, arisen in turn,This is not at all clear. It's base meaning in the old corpus is an 'era/aeon', which makes no sense in this context. According to the TL, it can maean 'fate'. This would work here - the heroine would understand that their argument was simly her lot in life, which would lessen the blame on the hero. In the attestation cited for this entry, I am not convinced that this is its meaning, and I have not found another example where it means that. This translation takes the meaning found in PN370, 'a turn', in this case of a new day. and counts me as a companion.

div.p: eṉpatu talaimakaḷ āṟṟāmai kaṇṭūṭal uṇarttac cellun tōḻi colliyatu.
After seeing the heroine unable to bear [the situation], the confidante, who had gone to resolve [the lovers'] quarrel, speaks [to the hero].

lg.l: Is it a good thing? It is not!
The anger of the one with the fragrant forehead
because of [the hero's] entrance with their ruddy-haired son
with a red marks and who wears a tāliThis is a specific amulet worn for protection..

div.p: eṉpatu tōḻi...

Cf. IA40: kātaṟ parattai ellārkku murittē ||
Cf. IA43: parattaiyiṟ pirinta kiḻavōṉ maṉaivi | pūppiṉ puṟappā ṭīraṟu nāḷu | nīttakaṉ ṟuṟaita laṟattā ṟaṉṟē ||
Cf. IAC43, p.179: aḵtāmāṟuː talaimakaṉ parattaiyiṟpirinta kālattut talaimakaṭkup pūpput tōṉṟiṟṟu. tōṉṟat talaimakaṉ uṇarum. eṅṅaṉam uṇarumōveṉiṉ vayilkaḷ uṇarttavē uṇarumeṉpatu.

Based on the size of the lost portion of C1, Cām. is a reasoble conjecture. It also, at least, mirrors a koḷu which one finds in later kōvai-s. Cf. Kalaicaikkōvai 410, composed in the 18th century, which UVC pulnished in 1935. This may have been his inspiration for the conjecture, apart from what makes sense in this poetic context.

It is not clear what exactly happended in C2. x varai nātaṉ ('the man from the land with the x mountains') is a common ephithet for the hero in Caṅkam and post-Caṅkam literature, but C1 very clearly reads akal vayal ūraṉ ('the man from the down with the vast paddy-fields'), which makes perfectly good sense and is attested in Kīḻkkaṇakku corpus, in Aintiṇai Aimpatu 23.1.

One has to assume the C1 reading is either the result of a misapplied sandhi, using the wrong intervocalic glide, or scribal error where the strong verbal root vicai-ttal ('to hasten'), was conjugated with the wrong suffix, or a k was missed out. The correct form should be vicaikkuvaṉ. If that was the indended reading, it is not clear what it would mean. UVC's emendation makes good sense and is minimal. Although incorrect glides are not generally a feature of C1, icaikuvaṉ ('I will speak') is most the plausible reading.

Eyes reddining is a common trope in Tamil poetry and considering the surrounding poems, all of which concern the anger of the heroine, cē-ttal is the more likely reading. cōrntaṉaḷ would also make sense though. In that case the eyes of the heroine would become dejected, as opposed to red (through either crying, anger, or both).

There is no reason by one would expect gemination here, and the only quasi-parallel I have found in the corpus of the C1 reading, is sometimes transmitted with gemination and sometimes without (Tirumuṟai 11.030.8), and there in a context which would not make sense in this poem. UVC's two proposed emendations, the first in C2 and the second in Cām. are hard to disambiguate. As I understand it, they both mean much the same - 'from today' (for a short discussion on other possibilites, see the note to the translation). ūḻiṉ has to be understood as a contracted form of ūḻiyiṉ. It is attested in PN237.10 and NA367.6, and reported as a variant to KT270.2 by Wilden. It is printed by UVC in his 1937 edition of the KT. I consider this the lectio difficilior when judged against C2.
